                                   5                          IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
                                   6                      FOR THE NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA
                                   7
                                   8        JOSEPH ANTHONY REYNA,                          Case No. 26-cv-06068-CRB
                                   9                    Plaintiff,
                                                                                           ORDER DENYING APPLICATION
                                  10             v.                                        FOR TEMPORARY RESTRAINING
                                                                                           ORDER; GRANTING
                                  11        THE WALT DISNEY COMPANY,                       APPLICATION TO PROCEED IN
                                                                                           FORMA PAUPERIS; SCREENING
                                  12                    Defendant.
Northern District of California




                                                                                           COMPLAINT
 United States District Court




                                  13           Plaintiff Joseph Reyna, proceeding pro se, filed a complaint against Defendant The
                                  14   Walt Disney Company (“Disney”), alleging that Disney misrepresented its livestream
                                  15   services. Compl. (dkt. 1). Reyna submitted an application for leave to proceed in forma
                                  16   pauperis (“IFP”). IFP (dkt. 4). He subsequently moved for a temporary restraining order
                                  17   (“TRO”) to enjoin Disney from routine data deletion. Mot. (dkt. 6). The Court DENIES
                                  18   Reyna’s motion for a TRO. The Court also GRANTS Reyan’s IFP application and
                                  19   screens the complaint.
                                  20   I.      TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDER
                                  21           Reyna seeks to enjoin Disney and suspend its automated deletion of electronically
                                  22   stored information. Mot. at 1. His motion fails to satisfy the high threshold required for a
                                  23   TRO.
                                  24           A TRO is an “extraordinary and drastic remedy.” Munaf v. Geren, 553 U.S. 674,
                                  25   689 (2008). A party seeking a TRO must establish: (1) a likelihood of success on the
                                  26   merits; (2) a likelihood of irreparable harm absent preliminary relief; (3) that the balance of
                                  27   equities tips in the plaintiff’s favor; and (4) that an injunction is in the public interest.
                                  28   Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 20 (2008). The “[l]ikelihood of success
                                         Case 3:26-cv-06068-CRB         Document 12        Filed 06/22/26   Page 2 of 4




                                   1   on the merits ‘is the most important Winter factor.’” Disney Enters., Inc. v. VidAngel,
                                   2   Inc., 869 F.3d 848, 856 (9th Cir. 2017) (quoting Garcia v. Google, Inc., 786 F.3d 733, 740
                                   3   (9th Cir. 2015)). A district court should enter a TRO only “upon a clear showing that the
                                   4   plaintiff is entitled to such relief.” Winter, 555 U.S. at 21.
                                   5          Reyna’s motion is dead on arrival. He fails to justify why this must be ex parte and
                                   6   does not address the Winter factors.
                                   7          For starters, Reyna’s motion is procedurally inappropriate. Federal Rule of Civil
                                   8   Procedure 65(b) provides that a court may issue a TRO without notice to the adverse party
                                   9   in limited circumstances where “specific facts in an affidavit or a verified complaint
                                  10   clearly show that immediate and irreparable injury, loss, or damage will result to the
                                  11   movant before the adverse party can be heard in opposition.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 65(b)(1)(A).
                                  12   The movant must also certify in writing any efforts made to give notice and the reasons
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   why it should not be required. Fed. R. Civ. P. 65(b)(1)(B). In cases where notice could
                                  14   have been given to the adverse party, courts have recognized “a very narrow band of cases
                                  15   in which ex parte orders are proper because notice to the defendant would render fruitless
                                  16   the further prosecution of the action.” Reno Air Racing Ass’n., Inc. v. McCord, 452 F.3d
                                  17   1126, 1131 (9th Cir. 2006) (internal quotation omitted). Applicants must do more than
                                  18   assert “that the adverse party would dispose of evidence if given notice.” Id. (citation
                                  19   modified). They must show that the defendant would have “disregarded a direct court
                                  20   order” and support the assertion by showing they have “a history of disposing of evidence
                                  21   or violating court orders.” Id. (citation modified).
                                  22          Reyna has not made such a showing. In his ex parte certification, he says he did not
                                  23   give prior notice because there could be a deletion cycle before a noticed motion, he had
                                  24   previously sent preservation demands that have gone unanswered, and notice could have
                                  25   caused intentional deletion. Mot. at 4. That justification does not meet the standard
                                  26   articulated in McCord—indeed, McCord explains that such reasoning would be
                                  27   insufficient.
                                  28          Moreover, besides irreparable harm, Reyna does not mention any of the Winter
                                                                                      2
                                         Case 3:26-cv-06068-CRB         Document 12        Filed 06/22/26   Page 3 of 4




                                   1   factors or explain why he is entitled to extraordinary relief. That alone is grounds for
                                   2   denial. See Felix Khosrovian v. D. Marin et al., 2026 WL 1508713, at *1 (C.D. Cal. Feb.
                                   3   2, 2026) (failure to “meaningfully address the Winter factors” warranted summary denial).
                                   4   Further, Reyna’s “delay in seeking relief weighs against granting a TRO.” Perez v. City of
                                   5   Petaluma, 2021 WL 3934327, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 13, 2021). He purports to be aware of
                                   6   Disney’s automated deletion cycles, even reaching out to Disney as latest as December
                                   7   2025 for document preservation. Mot. at 4. But he only filed this action—and his request
                                   8   for a TRO—months later. He does not explain why he could not have filed earlier.
                                   9   Reyna’s “unexplained delay in seeking relief undermines [his] claim that [he] will suffer
                                  10   irreparable harm in the absence of a TRO.” Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Zhu, 2026 WL
                                  11   915291, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 3, 2026).
                                  12          Accordingly, the Court DENIES Reyna’s motion for a TRO. The Court notes,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   however, that if Disney has engaged in any spoliation despite Reyna’s preservation letters,
                                  14   then it may be subject to sanctions. Katzman v. Los Angles Cnty. Metro. Transportation
                                  15   Auth., 2015 WL 13861765, at *9 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 26, 2015) (“Evidence of spoliation may
                                  16   be grounds for sanctions, including an adverse inference instruction.”).
                                  17   II.    IN FORMA PAUPERIS AND SCREENING
                                  18          The Court GRANTS Reyna’s application for leave to proceed IFP. The Court also
                                  19   screens the complaint as discussed below.
                                  20          IFP applications are governed by 28 U.S.C. § 1915, which provides in relevant part
                                  21   that “any court of the United States may authorize the commencement, prosecution or
                                  22   defense of any suit, action or proceeding, civil or criminal, or appeal therein, without
                                  23   prepayment of fees . . . by a person who submits an affidavit . . . that the person is unable
                                  24   to pay such fees.” 28 U.S.C. § 1915(a). When a district court grants IFP status, the court
                                  25   must screen the complaint and dismiss the action if it is frivolous. See id. § 1915(e)(2)(B);
                                  26   Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122, 1126– 27 & n.7 (9th Cir. 2000). If the complaint survives
                                  27   the initial screening, the court must “order that service be made by a United States marshal
                                  28   or deputy marshal or by a person specially appointed by the court.” Fed. R. Civ. P.
                                                                                      3
                                            Case 3:26-cv-06068-CRB      Document 12        Filed 06/22/26    Page 4 of 4




                                   1   4(c)(3).
                                   2           The Court grants Reyna’s IFP application based on the lack of financial resources
                                   3   documented in the affidavit accompanying the application. See IFP. The Court screens
                                   4   Reyna’s complaint and dismisses his third count. That claim is based on California’s
                                   5   Automatic Renewal Law (“ARL”). But “the ARL does not create a private right of
                                   6   action.” Wahl v. Yahoo! Inc., 2018 WL 6002323, at *1 (N.D. Cal. Nov. 15, 2018).
                                   7   Accordingly, the Court dismisses the claim with prejudice.
                                   8           The Court orders the Clerk of Court to carry out service of process on Disney and
                                   9   mail a copy of this order to Reyna at the address he has provided on the docket.1
                                  10           IT IS SO ORDERED.
                                  11           Dated: June 22, 2026
                                                                                          CHARLES R. BREYER
                                  12                                                      United States District Judge
Northern District of California
 United States District Court
